# MPM H21 Masterclass Overview

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nD183jP3H4Y)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video introduces the Houdini 21 MPM Masterclass, a follow-up to the Houdini 20.5 masterclass presented by Alex Wevinger. It is not an introductory tutorial -- it assumes working knowledge of the MPM solver at a user level. The video provides an outline of all topics covered across the 18-part series, including new solver features, new post-simulation workflow nodes, and practical demo scenes using real-world setups.

## Key Concepts

### New Solver Features in Houdini 21

The MPM solver in Houdini 21 introduces several significant new features:

- **Surface Tension** -- A new surface tension model has been added to the MPM solver, enabling effects like water droplets holding their shape on surfaces.
- **Auto Sleep Mechanism** -- An optimization feature that deactivates particles that have come to rest, significantly speeding up simulations where large portions of the material are stationary.
- **Continuous Emission Expansion** -- Allows sourcing new material on top of existing material to create internal pressure effects. This is useful for scenarios where material needs to be continuously added during simulation.
- **Per-Voxel Varying Friction and Stickiness** -- Provides per-voxel control over friction and stickiness on colliders, replacing the Houdini 20.5 workaround of duplicating colliders with different friction values.
- **Improved Deforming Colliders** -- Significant improvements to how the solver handles deforming collision geometry.

### Post-Simulation Workflow Nodes

A suite of new nodes has been introduced to streamline the post-simulation pipeline:

- **Surfacing nodes** -- Help convert the MPM particle simulation into mesh surfaces.
- **Debris emission nodes** -- Generate debris based on where the material is fracturing during simulation.
- **Rigid body dynamics replication nodes** -- Two nodes that work together to replicate rigid body dynamics workflows. This enables simulating very stiff materials (such as concrete) with MPM, then fracturing the original high-resolution asset based on the final simulation state and retargeting the MPM dynamics onto the fractured geometry.

### RBD-Style Workflow with MPM

The series covers a workflow for using MPM to handle stiff material destruction (like concrete or stone):

1. Run the MPM simulation on stiff material.
2. Extract the last state of the MPM sim.
3. Use that state to fracture the original high-resolution asset.
4. Retarget the dynamics of the MPM simulation onto the post-fractured asset.

This provides the physical accuracy of MPM with the visual quality of traditional RBD fracture workflows.

### Practical Demo Scenes

The masterclass includes walkthrough demonstrations of all the scenes shown at the beginning of the presentation. These are not built from scratch but are examined in detail, highlighting the important parts of each setup to show how new features and nodes are applied in practical, real-world scenarios. All assets and HIP files are provided for download.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Solver | Core simulation solver with new H21 features | Surface tension, auto sleep, collision settings |
| MPM Configure | Initial setup recipe for MPM simulations | Particle separation, material presets |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry for the solver | Friction, stickiness, resolution override |
| MPM Source | Sources material into the simulation | Material preset, surface tension phase |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Set up MPM Configure** -- Begin every MPM setup with the MPM Configure node to establish the simulation framework.
2. **Define sources and colliders** -- Connect source geometry through MPM Source and collision geometry through MPM Collider.
3. **Configure solver features** -- Enable new H21 features on the MPM Solver as needed (surface tension, auto sleep, etc.).
4. **Run simulation** -- Simulate and iterate on parameters.
5. **Post-process with new nodes** -- Use the new surfacing, debris, and retargeting nodes to prepare simulation output for rendering.

## Tips & Insights

- This masterclass assumes you already know how the MPM solver works at a basic level. If you are new to MPM, start with the Houdini 20.5 MPM masterclass first.
- Per-voxel friction and stickiness eliminates the 20.5 workaround of duplicating colliders, making setups cleaner and more art-directable.
- The RBD-style retargeting workflow allows combining MPM's physical accuracy with high-resolution fractured geometry for final renders.
- All demo HIP files and assets are available for download so you can follow along or study setups independently.

# MPM Surface Tension

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video demonstrates the new surface tension feature added to the MPM solver in Houdini 21. It covers two implementation methods -- point-based and grid-based -- along with a multiphase system that allows different materials to have independent surface tension properties. The tutorial walks through practical examples including water droplets on leaves (macro-scale surface tension) and objects emerging from liquid (drip/tendril effects), showing how to tune friction, stickiness, and surface tension strength for realistic results.

## Key Concepts

### Point-Based Surface Tension (Default Method)

The default surface tension implementation in the MPM solver is point-based. This is the same implementation used in Vellum. Each particle examines its neighbors to compute surface tension forces, meaning the resolution of the surface tension effect scales with the resolution of the point cloud.

**Characteristics:**
- Most stable implementation of surface tension in MPM.
- More expensive computationally than the grid-based method.
- Requires more VRAM on GPU because each point must be aware of all its neighbors, so memory usage grows quickly with particle count.
- Produces reliable, predictable results at the cost of performance.

### Grid-Based Surface Tension

An alternative implementation that computes surface tension on the MPM grid rather than on individual particles.

**Characteristics:**
- Significantly faster than the point-based method. [12:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=728)
- Less stable -- can produce unmotivated velocity gains where blobs of water start moving in unexpected directions.
- Well-suited for effects where extreme accuracy is not critical, such as drips falling from objects back into a body of water, or tendrils of liquid forming as objects emerge from water.
- Produces visually appealing tendril and droplet formation effects. [12:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=758)

### Multiphase Surface Tension

The MPM solver supports assigning different surface tension strengths and phase IDs per material. This enables multiple liquid materials in the same simulation where surface tension only applies within each material, not between them.

**How it works:**
- Each MPM Source node has a **surface tension** strength parameter and a **phase** parameter.
- Materials with the same phase value attract each other via surface tension. Materials with different phase values do not.
- The phase value acts as a material ID -- set phase=1 for one material and phase=2 for another to prevent cross-material surface tension. [7:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=439)
- The **surface tension strength** on the MPM Solver becomes a global multiplier on top of the per-source surface tension values. [9:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=571)

**Grid interpolation caveat:** Because all MPM materials share the same underlying grid, velocity and momentum transfer between phases can cause minor cross-contamination. A particle with zero surface tension located near particles with high surface tension may receive some of that motion through grid interpolation. This is inherent to how MPM works and generally produces acceptable results. [8:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=508)

### Collider Resolution for Thin Geometry

When working with thin collision geometry (such as leaves), the default MPM collider resolution may be insufficient. The collider resolution can be overridden directly on the MPM Collider node to ensure thin geometry is properly resolved. [1:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=94)

### Particle-Level Collision

By default, water may flow through thin colliders. Enabling **Particle Level Collision** on the MPM Solver (under the Collision tab) with the "Velocity Based Move Outside Collider" method prevents particles from passing through. [2:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=156)

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Initial setup recipe for every MPM scene | Particle separation |
| MPM Source | Defines source material with per-material controls | Preset (water), Surface Tension strength, Phase ID |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry | Resolution override, Friction, Stickiness, Detection Distance |
| MPM Solver | Core solver with surface tension toggle | Surface Tension (enable), Method (Point-Based / Grid-Based), Surface Tension Strength (global multiplier), Collision tab: Particle Level Collision, Velocity Based Move Outside Collider |

# MPM Auto Sleep

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video covers the auto sleep mechanism added to the MPM solver in Houdini 21, a performance optimization feature that deactivates particles at rest and reactivates them when disturbed. Two practical use cases are demonstrated: a large-scale spaceship erupting from the ground (where auto sleep provides roughly 2x speedup by keeping stationary soil inactive), and a staged activation scenario where a character model (Crag) is held in an unbalanced pose until a collider impact propagates through the material via MPM substeps. The video explains the three particle states (active, passive, boundary), the velocity threshold and delay parameters, and when auto sleep helps versus hurts performance.

## Key Concepts

### Three Particle States

When auto sleep is enabled, every particle has a `state` attribute with one of three values:

| State | Value | Behavior |
|-------|-------|----------|
| **Active** | 1 | Fully simulated -- participates in all MPM updates and is integrated forward in time. |
| **Passive/Inactive** | 0 | Completely frozen -- not updated or moved. Ignored by the solver, which is what provides the performance gain. |
| **Boundary** | 2 | A hybrid state required by MPM's dual particle-grid representation. Boundary particles have their attributes updated (deformation gradient, velocity) but are never integrated forward in time -- they stay in place. This provides correct boundary conditions at the interface between active and passive regions. [4:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=254) |

The boundary state is essential because MPM requires voxels at the edge of the active region to have properly updated attributes for the particle-to-grid and grid-to-particle transfer to work correctly.

### Velocity Threshold

The **velocity threshold** parameter controls the speed below which a particle is eligible for deactivation. This is a scalar speed value (not a vector), and it is **scale-dependent**:

- For small scenes, the default value may work.
- For large scenes (e.g., 100m+ across), multiply the threshold significantly (e.g., 10x). [3:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=193)

A higher threshold makes the sleep mechanism more aggressive -- particles are deactivated more readily.

### Delay Parameter

The **delay** parameter specifies the time in seconds that a particle must remain below the velocity threshold before it is deactivated. At 24 FPS with the default 0.5 second delay, a particle must be below the speed threshold for 12 consecutive frames before being put to sleep. [3:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=193)

### Reactivation via Substep Propagation

One of the most powerful aspects of auto sleep is how it interacts with MPM's high substep counts. When a collider impacts passive material:

1. On the first substep after impact, only the particles directly at the contact point are reactivated.
2. Those newly active particles exceed the velocity threshold and activate their neighbors on the next substep.
3. This chain reaction propagates through the material across all substeps within a single frame.

With high substep counts (e.g., 226 substeps as shown in the demo), an impact wave can propagate through an entire model within a single frame, activating everything nearly instantaneously. [9:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=566)

### Staged Activation Use Case

Auto sleep enables a "staged activation" workflow where a model starts fully passive (frozen in place) regardless of whether its pose is physically stable. The material only becomes active when an external force (such as a collider impact) disturbs it. This is demonstrated with the Crag character model held in an unbalanced standing pose -- without auto sleep, Crag falls over immediately. With auto sleep enabled, Crag remains frozen until a collider strikes his knee, at which point the impact propagates through all substeps and the entire body activates and responds to the collision. [7:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=441)

### Performance Characteristics

Auto sleep provides the greatest benefit in scenes where a large proportion of particles are stationary for extended periods:

- **Best case:** Large scenes where activity is localized (e.g., spaceship emerging from ground -- most soil is static). The spaceship demo achieved approximately **2x speedup** over frames 1-250. [5:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=348)
- **Worst case:** Scenes where most particles are active throughout the entire frame range. In this case, auto sleep adds overhead (managing states, maintaining boundary particles) with no benefit, and can actually decrease performance. [6:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=378)
- **During high-activity frames:** When the collider is actively displacing material and most particles are active, the solver may run slower than without auto sleep due to the state management overhead. [5:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=317)

The speedup is highly scene-dependent. Use auto sleep when you know there will be significant idle periods in your simulation.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Initial setup recipe | Particle Separation (multiply by 10 for very large scenes) |
| MPM Solver | Core solver with auto sleep toggle | Auto Sleep (enable), Velocity Threshold (scale-dependent), Delay (seconds), Visualization: Color From Attribute = state |
| MPM Source | Sources material into the simulation | Material preset |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry | Animated Rigid Collider mode, Stiffness |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Start with MPM Configure** -- Set up the simulation framework. For very large scenes (100m+), multiply particle separation significantly (e.g., 10x) to keep point counts manageable. [0:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=35)
2. **Set up source and collider** -- Connect source geometry through MPM Source and collision geometry through MPM Collider. Use Animated Rigid Collider mode for moving objects.
3. **Enable auto sleep on the MPM Solver** -- Toggle the auto sleep checkbox on the solver node.
4. **Adjust velocity threshold** -- Scale the velocity threshold relative to your scene size. For large scenes, multiply by 10 or more. For staged activation scenarios, multiply by 2 for more aggressive deactivation. [8:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=535)
5. **Set the delay** -- Configure the delay in seconds. Default is 0.5s (12 frames at 24 FPS). Shorter delays deactivate faster.
6. **Visualize particle state** -- On the MPM Solver, set visualization to color from the `state` attribute with a range of 0-2. Active = green, Passive = purple, Boundary = red. [2:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=131)
7. **Iterate** -- Run the simulation and observe the state visualization. Check that particles are correctly sleeping and waking. Monitor FPS to confirm speedup during idle periods.

## Tips & Insights

- Auto sleep adds management overhead to the solver. Only use it when you expect significant portions of the material to be stationary for extended periods. If everything is active the entire time, you will get zero benefit and potentially slower performance. [6:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=378)
- The velocity threshold is scale-dependent. A value that works for a small tabletop scene will be far too small for a 100-meter landscape. Always scale it relative to your scene dimensions.
- Visualizing the `state` attribute (range 0-2) is essential for understanding what the solver is doing. The color coding (green = active, purple = passive, red = boundary) immediately reveals whether sleep is working as intended.
- The boundary state (red particles) is not a bug -- it is a necessary buffer zone that maintains correct physical behavior at the interface between active and passive regions.
- For staged activation, the high substep count in MPM is your ally. Impact waves propagate through substeps, so even with 200+ substeps per frame, a single collision event can activate an entire model within one frame. [9:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=596)

- After all activity ceases and particles progressively deactivate, simulation speed ramps up dramatically -- the Crag demo went from normal simulation speed to 13 FPS once everything settled.
- For the staged activation workflow, make sure to increase material stiffness if the geometry should behave as a solid when it activates. [8:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=503)

## Key Concepts

### Point-Based Surface Tension (Default Method)

The default surface tension implementation in the MPM solver is point-based. This is the same implementation used in Vellum. Each particle examines its neighbors to compute surface tension forces, meaning the resolution of the surface tension effect scales with the resolution of the point cloud.

**Characteristics:**
- Most stable implementation of surface tension in MPM.
- More expensive computationally than the grid-based method.
- Requires more VRAM on GPU because each point must be aware of all its neighbors, so memory usage grows quickly with particle count.
- Produces reliable, predictable results at the cost of performance.

### Grid-Based Surface Tension

An alternative implementation that computes surface tension on the MPM grid rather than on individual particles.

**Characteristics:**
- Significantly faster than the point-based method. [12:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=728)
- Less stable -- can produce unmotivated velocity gains where blobs of water start moving in unexpected directions.
- Well-suited for effects where extreme accuracy is not critical, such as drips falling from objects back into a body of water, or tendrils of liquid forming as objects emerge from water.
- Produces visually appealing tendril and droplet formation effects. [12:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=758)

### Multiphase Surface Tension

The MPM solver supports assigning different surface tension strengths and phase IDs per material. This enables multiple liquid materials in the same simulation where surface tension only applies within each material, not between them.

**How it works:**
- Each MPM Source node has a **surface tension** strength parameter and a **phase** parameter.
- Materials with the same phase value attract each other via surface tension. Materials with different phase values do not.
- The phase value acts as a material ID -- set phase=1 for one material and phase=2 for another to prevent cross-material surface tension. [7:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=439)
- The **surface tension strength** on the MPM Solver becomes a global multiplier on top of the per-source surface tension values. [9:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=571)

**Grid interpolation caveat:** Because all MPM materials share the same underlying grid, velocity and momentum transfer between phases can cause minor cross-contamination. A particle with zero surface tension located near particles with high surface tension may receive some of that motion through grid interpolation. This is inherent to how MPM works and generally produces acceptable results. [8:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=508)

### Collider Resolution for Thin Geometry

When working with thin collision geometry (such as leaves), the default MPM collider resolution may be insufficient. The collider resolution can be overridden directly on the MPM Collider node to ensure thin geometry is properly resolved. [1:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=94)

### Particle-Level Collision

By default, water may flow through thin colliders. Enabling **Particle Level Collision** on the MPM Solver (under the Collision tab) with the "Velocity Based Move Outside Collider" method prevents particles from passing through. [2:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=156)

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Initial setup recipe for every MPM scene | Particle separation |
| MPM Source | Defines source material with per-material controls | Preset (water), Surface Tension strength, Phase ID |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry | Resolution override, Friction, Stickiness, Detection Distance |
| MPM Solver | Core solver with surface tension toggle | Surface Tension (enable), Method (Point-Based / Grid-Based), Surface Tension Strength (global multiplier), Collision tab: Particle Level Collision, Velocity Based Move Outside Collider |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Start with MPM Configure** -- Drop an MPM Configure node to establish the simulation domain and base settings.
2. **Set up the collider** -- Connect collision geometry to an MPM Collider. For thin geometry, override the resolution on the collider node until the shape is properly resolved.
3. **Set up the source** -- Connect source geometry to an MPM Source and assign a material preset (e.g., water). Decrease particle separation for more resolution.
4. **Enable particle-level collision** -- On the MPM Solver, go to the Collision tab and enable Particle Level Collision with "Velocity Based Move Outside Collider" to prevent leaking. [2:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=156)
5. **Enable surface tension** -- On the MPM Solver, enable surface tension. Start with the point-based method for stability. Boost the strength value (try 5x or higher) to see visible effects. [4:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=248)
6. **Increase friction and stickiness** -- Set friction and stickiness to very high values on the collider to compensate for surface tension pushing particles away from the collider surface. [4:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=279)
7. **(Optional) Set up multiphase** -- Duplicate the MPM Source for each material. Assign different phase IDs and surface tension values per source. The solver's surface tension strength acts as a global multiplier.
8. **(Optional) Switch to grid-based** -- For drip/tendril effects where speed matters more than precision, switch to the grid-based method on the solver. Reduce friction slightly and increase stickiness. You can also multiply the detection distance (e.g., 2x) to improve collider adhesion. [11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=697)

## Tips & Insights

- Always start every MPM scene with MPM Configure -- it provides the foundational setup that all other MPM nodes expect.
- When using surface tension, you will likely need to set friction and stickiness to very high values because surface tension forces push particles slightly away from collider surfaces, creating a "levitation" effect. Crank these values aggressively. [5:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=310)
- The point-based method uses the same algorithm as Vellum's surface tension, making its behavior predictable if you are familiar with Vellum workflows.
- The grid-based method is much faster but can produce spontaneous velocity artifacts. Use it for effects like drips and tendrils where some instability is acceptable or even desirable.
- For the grid-based method, try increasing the collider detection distance (e.g., multiply by 2) to help particles adhere to surfaces. [11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=697)
- Multiphase setups are useful for look development -- creating magical or unusual liquid interactions where different materials behave independently.
- Visualize particles by sampling speed to better observe simulation behavior during playback. [2:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=126)
- For thin colliders, always check the collider resolution. If you cannot see the shape in the viewport, the solver cannot resolve it either.

# MPM Auto Sleep

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video covers the auto sleep mechanism added to the MPM solver in Houdini 21, a performance optimization feature that deactivates particles at rest and reactivates them when disturbed. Two practical use cases are demonstrated: a large-scale spaceship erupting from the ground (where auto sleep provides roughly 2x speedup by keeping stationary soil inactive), and a staged activation scenario where a character model (Crag) is held in an unbalanced pose until a collider impact propagates through the material via MPM substeps. The video explains the three particle states (active, passive, boundary), the velocity threshold and delay parameters, and when auto sleep helps versus hurts performance.

## Key Concepts

### Three Particle States

When auto sleep is enabled, every particle has a `state` attribute with one of three values:

| State | Value | Behavior |
|-------|-------|----------|
| **Active** | 1 | Fully simulated -- participates in all MPM updates and is integrated forward in time. |
| **Passive/Inactive** | 0 | Completely frozen -- not updated or moved. Ignored by the solver, which is what provides the performance gain. |
| **Boundary** | 2 | A hybrid state required by MPM's dual particle-grid representation. Boundary particles have their attributes updated (deformation gradient, velocity) but are never integrated forward in time -- they stay in place. This provides correct boundary conditions at the interface between active and passive regions. [4:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=254) |

The boundary state is essential because MPM requires voxels at the edge of the active region to have properly updated attributes for the particle-to-grid and grid-to-particle transfer to work correctly.

### Velocity Threshold

The **velocity threshold** parameter controls the speed below which a particle is eligible for deactivation. This is a scalar speed value (not a vector), and it is **scale-dependent**:

- For small scenes, the default value may work.
- For large scenes (e.g., 100m+ across), multiply the threshold significantly (e.g., 10x). [3:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=193)

A higher threshold makes the sleep mechanism more aggressive -- particles are deactivated more readily.

### Delay Parameter

The **delay** parameter specifies the time in seconds that a particle must remain below the velocity threshold before it is deactivated. At 24 FPS with the default 0.5 second delay, a particle must be below the speed threshold for 12 consecutive frames before being put to sleep. [3:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=193)

### Reactivation via Substep Propagation

One of the most powerful aspects of auto sleep is how it interacts with MPM's high substep counts. When a collider impacts passive material:

1. On the first substep after impact, only the particles directly at the contact point are reactivated.
2. Those newly active particles exceed the velocity threshold and activate their neighbors on the next substep.
3. This chain reaction propagates through the material across all substeps within a single frame.

With high substep counts (e.g., 226 substeps as shown in the demo), an impact wave can propagate through an entire model within a single frame, activating everything nearly instantaneously. [9:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=566)

### Staged Activation Use Case

Auto sleep enables a "staged activation" workflow where a model starts fully passive (frozen in place) regardless of whether its pose is physically stable. The material only becomes active when an external force (such as a collider impact) disturbs it. This is demonstrated with the Crag character model held in an unbalanced standing pose -- without auto sleep, Crag falls over immediately. With auto sleep enabled, Crag remains frozen until a collider strikes his knee, at which point the impact propagates through all substeps and the entire body activates and responds to the collision. [7:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=441)

### Performance Characteristics

Auto sleep provides the greatest benefit in scenes where a large proportion of particles are stationary for extended periods:

- **Best case:** Large scenes where activity is localized (e.g., spaceship emerging from ground -- most soil is static). The spaceship demo achieved approximately **2x speedup** over frames 1-250. [5:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=348)
- **Worst case:** Scenes where most particles are active throughout the entire frame range. In this case, auto sleep adds overhead (managing states, maintaining boundary particles) with no benefit, and can actually decrease performance. [6:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=378)
- **During high-activity frames:** When the collider is actively displacing material and most particles are active, the solver may run slower than without auto sleep due to the state management overhead. [5:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=317)

The speedup is highly scene-dependent. Use auto sleep when you know there will be significant idle periods in your simulation.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Initial setup recipe | Particle Separation (multiply by 10 for very large scenes) |
| MPM Solver | Core solver with auto sleep toggle | Auto Sleep (enable), Velocity Threshold (scale-dependent), Delay (seconds), Visualization: Color From Attribute = state |
| MPM Source | Sources material into the simulation | Material preset |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry | Animated Rigid Collider mode, Stiffness |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Start with MPM Configure** -- Set up the simulation framework. For very large scenes (100m+), multiply particle separation significantly (e.g., 10x) to keep point counts manageable. [0:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=35)
2. **Set up source and collider** -- Connect source geometry through MPM Source and collision geometry through MPM Collider. Use Animated Rigid Collider mode for moving objects.
3. **Enable auto sleep on the MPM Solver** -- Toggle the auto sleep checkbox on the solver node.
4. **Adjust velocity threshold** -- Scale the velocity threshold relative to your scene size. For large scenes, multiply by 10 or more. For staged activation scenarios, multiply by 2 for more aggressive deactivation. [8:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=535)
5. **Set the delay** -- Configure the delay in seconds. Default is 0.5s (12 frames at 24 FPS). Shorter delays deactivate faster.
6. **Visualize particle state** -- On the MPM Solver, set visualization to color from the `state` attribute with a range of 0-2. Active = green, Passive = purple, Boundary = red. [2:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=131)
7. **Iterate** -- Run the simulation and observe the state visualization. Check that particles are correctly sleeping and waking. Monitor FPS to confirm speedup during idle periods.

## Tips & Insights

- Auto sleep adds management overhead to the solver. Only use it when you expect significant portions of the material to be stationary for extended periods. If everything is active the entire time, you will get zero benefit and potentially slower performance. [6:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=378)
- The velocity threshold is scale-dependent. A value that works for a small tabletop scene will be far too small for a 100-meter landscape. Always scale it relative to your scene dimensions.
- Visualizing the `state` attribute (range 0-2) is essential for understanding what the solver is doing. The color coding (green = active, purple = passive, red = boundary) immediately reveals whether sleep is working as intended.
- The boundary state (red particles) is not a bug -- it is a necessary buffer zone that maintains correct physical behavior at the interface between active and passive regions.
- For staged activation, the high substep count in MPM is your ally. Impact waves propagate through substeps, so even with 200+ substeps per frame, a single collision event can activate an entire model within one frame. [9:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=596)
- The spaceship demo ran at 1.7-1.8 FPS without auto sleep and achieved roughly 2x speedup with auto sleep over the full frame range (1-250). During fully passive periods, FPS jumped to 13+. [10:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=659)
- After all activity ceases and particles progressively deactivate, simulation speed ramps up dramatically -- the Crag demo went from normal simulation speed to 13 FPS once everything settled.
- For the staged activation workflow, make sure to increase material stiffness if the geometry should behave as a solid when it activates. [8:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=503)

# MPM Surface Tension

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video demonstrates the new surface tension feature added to the MPM solver in Houdini 21. It covers two implementation methods -- point-based and grid-based -- along with a multiphase system that allows different materials to have independent surface tension properties. The tutorial walks through practical examples including water droplets on leaves (macro-scale surface tension) and objects emerging from liquid (drip/tendril effects), showing how to tune friction, stickiness, and surface tension strength for realistic results.

## Key Concepts

### Point-Based Surface Tension (Default Method)

The default surface tension implementation in the MPM solver is point-based. This is the same implementation used in Vellum. Each particle examines its neighbors to compute surface tension forces, meaning the resolution of the surface tension effect scales with the resolution of the point cloud.

**Characteristics:**
- Most stable implementation of surface tension in MPM.
- More expensive computationally than the grid-based method.
- Requires more VRAM on GPU because each point must be aware of all its neighbors, so memory usage grows quickly with particle count.
- Produces reliable, predictable results at the cost of performance.

### Grid-Based Surface Tension

An alternative implementation that computes surface tension on the MPM grid rather than on individual particles.

**Characteristics:**
- Significantly faster than the point-based method. [12:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=728)
- Less stable -- can produce unmotivated velocity gains where blobs of water start moving in unexpected directions.
- Well-suited for effects where extreme accuracy is not critical, such as drips falling from objects back into a body of water, or tendrils of liquid forming as objects emerge from water.
- Produces visually appealing tendril and droplet formation effects. [12:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=758)

### Multiphase Surface Tension

The MPM solver supports assigning different surface tension strengths and phase IDs per material. This enables multiple liquid materials in the same simulation where surface tension only applies within each material, not between them.

**How it works:**
- Each MPM Source node has a **surface tension** strength parameter and a **phase** parameter.
- Materials with the same phase value attract each other via surface tension. Materials with different phase values do not.
- The phase value acts as a material ID -- set phase=1 for one material and phase=2 for another to prevent cross-material surface tension. [7:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=439)
- The **surface tension strength** on the MPM Solver becomes a global multiplier on top of the per-source surface tension values. [9:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=571)

**Grid interpolation caveat:** Because all MPM materials share the same underlying grid, velocity and momentum transfer between phases can cause minor cross-contamination. A particle with zero surface tension located near particles with high surface tension may receive some of that motion through grid interpolation. This is inherent to how MPM works and generally produces acceptable results. [8:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=508)

### Collider Resolution for Thin Geometry

When working with thin collision geometry (such as leaves), the default MPM collider resolution may be insufficient. The collider resolution can be overridden directly on the MPM Collider node to ensure thin geometry is properly resolved. [1:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=94)

### Particle-Level Collision

By default, water may flow through thin colliders. Enabling **Particle Level Collision** on the MPM Solver (under the Collision tab) with the "Velocity Based Move Outside Collider" method prevents particles from passing through. [2:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=156)

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Initial setup recipe for every MPM scene | Particle separation |
| MPM Source | Defines source material with per-material controls | Preset (water), Surface Tension strength, Phase ID |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry | Resolution override, Friction, Stickiness, Detection Distance |
| MPM Solver | Core solver with surface tension toggle | Surface Tension (enable), Method (Point-Based / Grid-Based), Surface Tension Strength (global multiplier), Collision tab: Particle Level Collision, Velocity Based Move Outside Collider |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Start with MPM Configure** -- Drop an MPM Configure node to establish the simulation domain and base settings.
2. **Set up the collider** -- Connect collision geometry to an MPM Collider. For thin geometry, override the resolution on the collider node until the shape is properly resolved.
3. **Set up the source** -- Connect source geometry to an MPM Source and assign a material preset (e.g., water). Decrease particle separation for more resolution.
4. **Enable particle-level collision** -- On the MPM Solver, go to the Collision tab and enable Particle Level Collision with "Velocity Based Move Outside Collider" to prevent leaking. [2:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=156)
5. **Enable surface tension** -- On the MPM Solver, enable surface tension. Start with the point-based method for stability. Boost the strength value (try 5x or higher) to see visible effects. [4:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=248)
6. **Increase friction and stickiness** -- Set friction and stickiness to very high values on the collider to compensate for surface tension pushing particles away from the collider surface. [4:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=279)
7. **(Optional) Set up multiphase** -- Duplicate the MPM Source for each material. Assign different phase IDs and surface tension values per source. The solver's surface tension strength acts as a global multiplier.
8. **(Optional) Switch to grid-based** -- For drip/tendril effects where speed matters more than precision, switch to the grid-based method on the solver. Reduce friction slightly and increase stickiness. You can also multiply the detection distance (e.g., 2x) to improve collider adhesion. [11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=697)

## Tips & Insights

- Always start every MPM scene with MPM Configure -- it provides the foundational setup that all other MPM nodes expect.
- When using surface tension, you will likely need to set friction and stickiness to very high values because surface tension forces push particles slightly away from collider surfaces, creating a "levitation" effect. Crank these values aggressively. [5:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=310)
- The point-based method uses the same algorithm as Vellum's surface tension, making its behavior predictable if you are familiar with Vellum workflows.
- The grid-based method is much faster but can produce spontaneous velocity artifacts. Use it for effects like drips and tendrils where some instability is acceptable or even desirable.
- For the grid-based method, try increasing the collider detection distance (e.g., multiply by 2) to help particles adhere to surfaces. [11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=697)
- Multiphase setups are useful for look development -- creating magical or unusual liquid interactions where different materials behave independently.
- Visualize particles by sampling speed to better observe simulation behavior during playback. [2:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=126)
- For thin colliders, always check the collider resolution. If you cannot see the shape in the viewport, the solver cannot resolve it either.

# MPM Auto Sleep

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video covers the auto sleep mechanism added to the MPM solver in Houdini 21, a performance optimization feature that deactivates particles at rest and reactivates them when disturbed. Two practical use cases are demonstrated: a large-scale spaceship erupting from the ground (where auto sleep provides roughly 2x speedup by keeping stationary soil inactive), and a staged activation scenario where a character model (Crag) is held in an unbalanced pose until a collider impact propagates through the material via MPM substeps. The video explains the three particle states (active, passive, boundary), the velocity threshold and delay parameters, and when auto sleep helps versus hurts performance.

## Key Concepts

### Three Particle States

When auto sleep is enabled, every particle has a `state` attribute with one of three values:

| State | Value | Behavior |
|-------|-------|----------|
| **Active** | 1 | Fully simulated -- participates in all MPM updates and is integrated forward in time. |
| **Passive/Inactive** | 0 | Completely frozen -- not updated or moved. Ignored by the solver, which is what provides the performance gain. |
| **Boundary** | 2 | A hybrid state required by MPM's dual particle-grid representation. Boundary particles have their attributes updated (deformation gradient, velocity) but are never integrated forward in time -- they stay in place. This provides correct boundary conditions at the interface between active and passive regions. [4:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=254) |

The boundary state is essential because MPM requires voxels at the edge of the active region to have properly updated attributes for the particle-to-grid and grid-to-particle transfer to work correctly.

### Velocity Threshold

The **velocity threshold** parameter controls the speed below which a particle is eligible for deactivation. This is a scalar speed value (not a vector), and it is **scale-dependent**:

- For small scenes, the default value may work.
- For large scenes (e.g., 100m+ across), multiply the threshold significantly (e.g., 10x). [3:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=193)

A higher threshold makes the sleep mechanism more aggressive -- particles are deactivated more readily.

### Delay Parameter

The **delay** parameter specifies the time in seconds that a particle must remain below the velocity threshold before it is deactivated. At 24 FPS with the default 0.5 second delay, a particle must be below the speed threshold for 12 consecutive frames before being put to sleep. [3:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=193)

### Reactivation via Substep Propagation

One of the most powerful aspects of auto sleep is how it interacts with MPM's high substep counts. When a collider impacts passive material:

1. On the first substep after impact, only the particles directly at the contact point are reactivated.
2. Those newly active particles exceed the velocity threshold and activate their neighbors on the next substep.
3. This chain reaction propagates through the material across all substeps within a single frame.

With high substep counts (e.g., 226 substeps as shown in the demo), an impact wave can propagate through an entire model within a single frame, activating everything nearly instantaneously. [9:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=566)

### Staged Activation Use Case

Auto sleep enables a "staged activation" workflow where a model starts fully passive (frozen in place) regardless of whether its pose is physically stable. The material only becomes active when an external force (such as a collider impact) disturbs it. This is demonstrated with the Crag character model held in an unbalanced standing pose -- without auto sleep, Crag falls over immediately. With auto sleep enabled, Crag remains frozen until a collider strikes his knee, at which point the impact propagates through all substeps and the entire body activates and responds to the collision. [7:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=441)

### Performance Characteristics

Auto sleep provides the greatest benefit in scenes where a large proportion of particles are stationary for extended periods:

- **Best case:** Large scenes where activity is localized (e.g., spaceship emerging from ground -- most soil is static). The spaceship demo achieved approximately **2x speedup** over frames 1-250. [5:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=348)
- **Worst case:** Scenes where most particles are active throughout the entire frame range. In this case, auto sleep adds overhead (managing states, maintaining boundary particles) with no benefit, and can actually decrease performance. [6:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=378)
- **During high-activity frames:** When the collider is actively displacing material and most particles are active, the solver may run slower than without auto sleep due to the state management overhead. [5:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=317)

The speedup is highly scene-dependent. Use auto sleep when you know there will be significant idle periods in your simulation.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Initial setup recipe | Particle Separation (multiply by 10 for very large scenes) |
| MPM Solver | Core solver with auto sleep toggle | Auto Sleep (enable), Velocity Threshold (scale-dependent), Delay (seconds), Visualization: Color From Attribute = state |
| MPM Source | Sources material into the simulation | Material preset |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry | Animated Rigid Collider mode, Stiffness |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Start with MPM Configure** -- Set up the simulation framework. For very large scenes (100m+), multiply particle separation significantly (e.g., 10x) to keep point counts manageable. [0:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=35)
2. **Set up source and collider** -- Connect source geometry through MPM Source and collision geometry through MPM Collider. Use Animated Rigid Collider mode for moving objects.
3. **Enable auto sleep on the MPM Solver** -- Toggle the auto sleep checkbox on the solver node.
4. **Adjust velocity threshold** -- Scale the velocity threshold relative to your scene size. For large scenes, multiply by 10 or more. For staged activation scenarios, multiply by 2 for more aggressive deactivation. [8:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=535)
5. **Set the delay** -- Configure the delay in seconds. Default is 0.5s (12 frames at 24 FPS). Shorter delays deactivate faster.
6. **Visualize particle state** -- On the MPM Solver, set visualization to color from the `state` attribute with a range of 0-2. Active = green, Passive = purple, Boundary = red. [2:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=131)
7. **Iterate** -- Run the simulation and observe the state visualization. Check that particles are correctly sleeping and waking. Monitor FPS to confirm speedup during idle periods.

## Tips & Insights

- Auto sleep adds management overhead to the solver. Only use it when you expect significant portions of the material to be stationary for extended periods. If everything is active the entire time, you will get zero benefit and potentially slower performance. [6:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=378)
- The velocity threshold is scale-dependent. A value that works for a small tabletop scene will be far too small for a 100-meter landscape. Always scale it relative to your scene dimensions.
- Visualizing the `state` attribute (range 0-2) is essential for understanding what the solver is doing. The color coding (green = active, purple = passive, red = boundary) immediately reveals whether sleep is working as intended.
- The boundary state (red particles) is not a bug -- it is a necessary buffer zone that maintains correct physical behavior at the interface between active and passive regions.
- For staged activation, the high substep count in MPM is your ally. Impact waves propagate through substeps, so even with 200+ substeps per frame, a single collision event can activate an entire model within one frame. [9:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=596)
- The spaceship demo ran at 1.7-1.8 FPS without auto sleep and achieved roughly 2x speedup with auto sleep over the full frame range (1-250). During fully passive periods, FPS jumped to 13+. [10:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=659)
- After all activity ceases and particles progressively deactivate, simulation speed ramps up dramatically -- the Crag demo went from normal simulation speed to 13 FPS once everything settled.
- For the staged activation workflow, make sure to increase material stiffness if the geometry should behave as a solid when it activates. [8:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=503)

# MPM Surface Tension

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video demonstrates the new surface tension feature added to the MPM solver in Houdini 21. It covers two implementation methods -- point-based and grid-based -- along with a multiphase system that allows different materials to have independent surface tension properties. The tutorial walks through practical examples including water droplets on leaves (macro-scale surface tension) and objects emerging from liquid (drip/tendril effects), showing how to tune friction, stickiness, and surface tension strength for realistic results.

## Key Concepts

### Point-Based Surface Tension (Default Method)

The default surface tension implementation in the MPM solver is point-based. This is the same implementation used in Vellum. Each particle examines its neighbors to compute surface tension forces, meaning the resolution of the surface tension effect scales with the resolution of the point cloud.

**Characteristics:**
- Most stable implementation of surface tension in MPM.
- More expensive computationally than the grid-based method.
- Requires more VRAM on GPU because each point must be aware of all its neighbors, so memory usage grows quickly with particle count.
- Produces reliable, predictable results at the cost of performance.

### Grid-Based Surface Tension

An alternative implementation that computes surface tension on the MPM grid rather than on individual particles.

**Characteristics:**
- Significantly faster than the point-based method. [12:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=728)
- Less stable -- can produce unmotivated velocity gains where blobs of water start moving in unexpected directions.
- Well-suited for effects where extreme accuracy is not critical, such as drips falling from objects back into a body of water, or tendrils of liquid forming as objects emerge from water.
- Produces visually appealing tendril and droplet formation effects. [12:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=758)

### Multiphase Surface Tension

The MPM solver supports assigning different surface tension strengths and phase IDs per material. This enables multiple liquid materials in the same simulation where surface tension only applies within each material, not between them.

**How it works:**
- Each MPM Source node has a **surface tension** strength parameter and a **phase** parameter.
- Materials with the same phase value attract each other via surface tension. Materials with different phase values do not.
- The phase value acts as a material ID -- set phase=1 for one material and phase=2 for another to prevent cross-material surface tension. [7:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=439)
- The **surface tension strength** on the MPM Solver becomes a global multiplier on top of the per-source surface tension values. [9:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=571)

**Grid interpolation caveat:** Because all MPM materials share the same underlying grid, velocity and momentum transfer between phases can cause minor cross-contamination. A particle with zero surface tension located near particles with high surface tension may receive some of that motion through grid interpolation. This is inherent to how MPM works and generally produces acceptable results. [8:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=508)

### Collider Resolution for Thin Geometry

When working with thin collision geometry (such as leaves), the default MPM collider resolution may be insufficient. The collider resolution can be overridden directly on the MPM Collider node to ensure thin geometry is properly resolved. [1:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=94)

### Particle-Level Collision

By default, water may flow through thin colliders. Enabling **Particle Level Collision** on the MPM Solver (under the Collision tab) with the "Velocity Based Move Outside Collider" method prevents particles from passing through. [2:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=156)

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Initial setup recipe for every MPM scene | Particle separation |
| MPM Source | Defines source material with per-material controls | Preset (water), Surface Tension strength, Phase ID |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry | Resolution override, Friction, Stickiness, Detection Distance |
| MPM Solver | Core solver with surface tension toggle | Surface Tension (enable), Method (Point-Based / Grid-Based), Surface Tension Strength (global multiplier), Collision tab: Particle Level Collision, Velocity Based Move Outside Collider |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Start with MPM Configure** -- Drop an MPM Configure node to establish the simulation domain and base settings.
2. **Set up the collider** -- Connect collision geometry to an MPM Collider. For thin geometry, override the resolution on the collider node until the shape is properly resolved.
3. **Set up the source** -- Connect source geometry to an MPM Source and assign a material preset (e.g., water). Decrease particle separation for more resolution.
4. **Enable particle-level collision** -- On the MPM Solver, go to the Collision tab and enable Particle Level Collision with "Velocity Based Move Outside Collider" to prevent leaking. [2:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=156)
5. **Enable surface tension** -- On the MPM Solver, enable surface tension. Start with the point-based method for stability. Boost the strength value (try 5x or higher) to see visible effects. [4:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=248)
6. **Increase friction and stickiness** -- Set friction and stickiness to very high values on the collider to compensate for surface tension pushing particles away from the collider surface. [4:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=279)
7. **(Optional) Set up multiphase** -- Duplicate the MPM Source for each material. Assign different phase IDs and surface tension values per source. The solver's surface tension strength acts as a global multiplier.
8. **(Optional) Switch to grid-based** -- For drip/tendril effects where speed matters more than precision, switch to the grid-based method on the solver. Reduce friction slightly and increase stickiness. You can also multiply the detection distance (e.g., 2x) to improve collider adhesion. [11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=697)

## Tips & Insights

- Always start every MPM scene with MPM Configure -- it provides the foundational setup that all other MPM nodes expect.
- When using surface tension, you will likely need to set friction and stickiness to very high values because surface tension forces push particles slightly away from collider surfaces, creating a "levitation" effect. Crank these values aggressively. [5:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=310)
- The point-based method uses the same algorithm as Vellum's surface tension, making its behavior predictable if you are familiar with Vellum workflows.
- The grid-based method is much faster but can produce spontaneous velocity artifacts. Use it for effects like drips and tendrils where some instability is acceptable or even desirable.
- For the grid-based method, try increasing the collider detection distance (e.g., multiply by 2) to help particles adhere to surfaces. [11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=697)
- Multiphase setups are useful for look development -- creating magical or unusual liquid interactions where different materials behave independently.
- Visualize particles by sampling speed to better observe simulation behavior during playback. [2:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HAv1t7q7VRk&t=126)
- For thin colliders, always check the collider resolution. If you cannot see the shape in the viewport, the solver cannot resolve it either.

# MPM Auto Sleep

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video covers the auto sleep mechanism added to the MPM solver in Houdini 21, a performance optimization feature that deactivates particles at rest and reactivates them when disturbed. Two practical use cases are demonstrated: a large-scale spaceship erupting from the ground (where auto sleep provides roughly 2x speedup by keeping stationary soil inactive), and a staged activation scenario where a character model (Crag) is held in an unbalanced pose until a collider impact propagates through the material via MPM substeps. The video explains the three particle states (active, passive, boundary), the velocity threshold and delay parameters, and when auto sleep helps versus hurts performance.

## Key Concepts

### Three Particle States

When auto sleep is enabled, every particle has a `state` attribute with one of three values:

| State | Value | Behavior |
|-------|-------|----------|
| **Active** | 1 | Fully simulated -- participates in all MPM updates and is integrated forward in time. |
| **Passive/Inactive** | 0 | Completely frozen -- not updated or moved. Ignored by the solver, which is what provides the performance gain. |
| **Boundary** | 2 | A hybrid state required by MPM's dual particle-grid representation. Boundary particles have their attributes updated (deformation gradient, velocity) but are never integrated forward in time -- they stay in place. This provides correct boundary conditions at the interface between active and passive regions. [4:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=254) |

The boundary state is essential because MPM requires voxels at the edge of the active region to have properly updated attributes for the particle-to-grid and grid-to-particle transfer to work correctly.

### Velocity Threshold

The **velocity threshold** parameter controls the speed below which a particle is eligible for deactivation. This is a scalar speed value (not a vector), and it is **scale-dependent**:

- For small scenes, the default value may work.
- For large scenes (e.g., 100m+ across), multiply the threshold significantly (e.g., 10x). [3:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=193)

A higher threshold makes the sleep mechanism more aggressive -- particles are deactivated more readily.

### Delay Parameter

The **delay** parameter specifies the time in seconds that a particle must remain below the velocity threshold before it is deactivated. At 24 FPS with the default 0.5 second delay, a particle must be below the speed threshold for 12 consecutive frames before being put to sleep. [3:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=193)

### Reactivation via Substep Propagation

One of the most powerful aspects of auto sleep is how it interacts with MPM's high substep counts. When a collider impacts passive material:

1. On the first substep after impact, only the particles directly at the contact point are reactivated.
2. Those newly active particles exceed the velocity threshold and activate their neighbors on the next substep.
3. This chain reaction propagates through the material across all substeps within a single frame.

With high substep counts (e.g., 226 substeps as shown in the demo), an impact wave can propagate through an entire model within a single frame, activating everything nearly instantaneously. [9:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=566)

### Staged Activation Use Case

Auto sleep enables a "staged activation" workflow where a model starts fully passive (frozen in place) regardless of whether its pose is physically stable. The material only becomes active when an external force (such as a collider impact) disturbs it. This is demonstrated with the Crag character model held in an unbalanced standing pose -- without auto sleep, Crag falls over immediately. With auto sleep enabled, Crag remains frozen until a collider strikes his knee, at which point the impact propagates through all substeps and the entire body activates and responds to the collision. [7:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=441)

### Performance Characteristics

Auto sleep provides the greatest benefit in scenes where a large proportion of particles are stationary for extended periods:

- **Best case:** Large scenes where activity is localized (e.g., spaceship emerging from ground -- most soil is static). The spaceship demo achieved approximately **2x speedup** over frames 1-250. [5:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=348)
- **Worst case:** Scenes where most particles are active throughout the entire frame range. In this case, auto sleep adds overhead (managing states, maintaining boundary particles) with no benefit, and can actually decrease performance. [6:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=378)
- **During high-activity frames:** When the collider is actively displacing material and most particles are active, the solver may run slower than without auto sleep due to the state management overhead. [5:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=317)

The speedup is highly scene-dependent. Use auto sleep when you know there will be significant idle periods in your simulation.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Initial setup recipe | Particle Separation (multiply by 10 for very large scenes) |
| MPM Solver | Core solver with auto sleep toggle | Auto Sleep (enable), Velocity Threshold (scale-dependent), Delay (seconds), Visualization: Color From Attribute = state |
| MPM Source | Sources material into the simulation | Material preset |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry | Animated Rigid Collider mode, Stiffness |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Start with MPM Configure** -- Set up the simulation framework. For very large scenes (100m+), multiply particle separation significantly (e.g., 10x) to keep point counts manageable. [0:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=35)
2. **Set up source and collider** -- Connect source geometry through MPM Source and collision geometry through MPM Collider. Use Animated Rigid Collider mode for moving objects.
3. **Enable auto sleep on the MPM Solver** -- Toggle the auto sleep checkbox on the solver node.
4. **Adjust velocity threshold** -- Scale the velocity threshold relative to your scene size. For large scenes, multiply by 10 or more. For staged activation scenarios, multiply by 2 for more aggressive deactivation. [8:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=535)
5. **Set the delay** -- Configure the delay in seconds. Default is 0.5s (12 frames at 24 FPS). Shorter delays deactivate faster.
6. **Visualize particle state** -- On the MPM Solver, set visualization to color from the `state` attribute with a range of 0-2. Active = green, Passive = purple, Boundary = red. [2:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=131)
7. **Iterate** -- Run the simulation and observe the state visualization. Check that particles are correctly sleeping and waking. Monitor FPS to confirm speedup during idle periods.

## Tips & Insights

- Auto sleep adds management overhead to the solver. Only use it when you expect significant portions of the material to be stationary for extended periods. If everything is active the entire time, you will get zero benefit and potentially slower performance. [6:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=378)
- The velocity threshold is scale-dependent. A value that works for a small tabletop scene will be far too small for a 100-meter landscape. Always scale it relative to your scene dimensions.
- Visualizing the `state` attribute (range 0-2) is essential for understanding what the solver is doing. The color coding (green = active, purple = passive, red = boundary) immediately reveals whether sleep is working as intended.
- The boundary state (red particles) is not a bug -- it is a necessary buffer zone that maintains correct physical behavior at the interface between active and passive regions.
- For staged activation, the high substep count in MPM is your ally. Impact waves propagate through substeps, so even with 200+ substeps per frame, a single collision event can activate an entire model within one frame. [9:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=596)
- The spaceship demo ran at 1.7-1.8 FPS without auto sleep and achieved roughly 2x speedup with auto sleep over the full frame range (1-250). During fully passive periods, FPS jumped to 13+. [10:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=659)
- After all activity ceases and particles progressively deactivate, simulation speed ramps up dramatically -- the Crag demo went from normal simulation speed to 13 FPS once everything settled.
- For the staged activation workflow, make sure to increase material stiffness if the geometry should behave as a solid when it activates. [8:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MwSsXRof_7Y&t=503)
